title: Confusion about Flávio Bolsonaro's whereabouts after Brazil cancels his passports
description: There is confusion about the whereabouts of defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, after Brazil cancelled his passports and Argen
body: There is confusion about the whereabouts of defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, after Brazil cancelled his passports and Argentine officials say he boarded a flight to Ecuador.Sources had told the BBC earlier on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had arrived in the US.But Argentine migration authorities later said he had crossed Brazil's land border with Argentina late on Tuesday night local time.In a tweet, external, the migration authorities said that he, his wife and two daughters had boarded a private flight headed towards the city of Guayaquil in Ecuador shortly after crossing the border.It is not clear whether Ecuador would be his final destination.Earlier on Tuesday, a senior US official confirmed the US State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the country, were they to request them.When reporters asked US President Donald Trump about Bolsonaro and his family's whereabouts later, he said: "I heard he was in Argentina."Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts started hours after Brazil's Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports amid an investigation into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro has not been charged and has denied the allegations.The court gave Bolsonaro a deadline of 24 hours to hand over the documents.At the time, Bolsonaro said he had no plans to leave the country, and insisted that he would stay in Brazil to lead the opposition to his left-wing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who on Sunday won the election. After he missed the deadline - at around noon local time (15:00 GMT) on Tuesday - Brazilian officials cancelled the documents.  When BBC Brasil contacted his lawyers, shortly after the deadline to hand over his passports had expired, they insisted they were "completely in the dark" about his whereabouts.Referring to speculation he had left the country, they said that "we knew nothing about this, and we still have no information about what happened," one lawyer said.A police source told the BBC that Brazilian federal officials were checking border crossings to establish if Bolsonaro could have travelled to neighbouring Argentina.At the time, Argentine authorities told the BBC there was no record of the senator entering their country through any border crossing.Bolsonaro has not made any public statements since Monday afternoon local time, when he posted a video on social media. He was already under investigation for alleged corruption over the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup and is under house arrest.A separate inquiry involves alleged links to a Brazilian lawyer, who is accused of laundering more than $1bn through a fraud scheme. Police said earlier this month they had discovered Bolsonaro had access to the bank accounts of a company owned by the lawyer.Bolsonaro denied doing business with the lawyer, and described the passport confiscation as an attempt to intimidate him.In addition to that investigation, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered police on Tuesday to examine Bolsonaro's electoral campaign over alleged foreign funding.The 45-year-old senator suffered a stinging defeat on Sunday when he was beaten by Lula in a presidential run-off, which Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win. His younger brother Eduardo Bolsonaro lives in the Texas, in the US, but was in Miami on Sunday, where he cast his vote at a polling station and attended an election viewing event which was streamed to his followers.Opinion polls had put him narrowly ahead of Lula and analysts pointed out that Bolsonaro's win in the first round of the election on 4 October, meant he was likely to take victory in the run-off.But after an early lead in the count, he was overtaken by the veteran incumbent, who became the first presidential candidate to overturn a first round loss to win in the second round. Lula won 51.79% of the vote, compared to Bolsonaro's 48.21%.Despite trailing by 4.4 million votes, Bolsonaro has not conceded and has called for the election to be annulled. He argues that he was put at a disadvantage because polling was extended by two hours on election day - even though the extension was requested by both his party and that of his rival.He called the extension, which was ordered by a Supreme Court justice, a "dirty trick".However the party he represented, the Liberal Party, has accepted the result, although it did say that the extension of voting "merits investigation".Ayelén Oliva,  Vinícius Mendes, Cecilia Barria Ricardo Senra and Ione Wells contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Confusion about Flávio Bolsonaro's whereabouts after Brazil cancels his passports

title: Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises
description: Two quotes from the chancellor and the prime minister get to the heart of this Budget."The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now… Br
body: Two quotes from the chancellor and the prime minister get to the heart of this Budget."The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now… Britain has it harder now," Chancellor John Healey said last month.And from Andy Burnham, days before he became prime minister: "This change... is the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years."So what happens when the economic realities confront the political ambitions of this new government?As Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), puts it, external: "We have a relatively new government with seemingly big ambitions but facing a long list of constraints."Some of those constraints… are self imposed, others are being worsened by global events, most noticeably war in the Middle East."Let's be clear, plenty in Westminster in all parties will say that the amount of money around isn't everything – how well taxpayers' money is spent and where it is spent matters too. And spending less and taxing less, plenty argue, should be a priority.But in the bones of many in the Labour Party is an instinct that the government, the state, can and should be a vital agent in driving change and improvements in people's lives – a world-view grounded in a sense that governments should proudly step in, rather than one that believes they should get out of the way.And how do you deliver a proudly proactive state, delivering for people in a noticeable way, when the tax burden is generationally high, the national debt is sky high, energy bills are rising and inflation is higher than expected? In short: it is not easy.But ministers argue all of this doesn't mean the government is powerless.Many are expecting support on the cost of living, and in particular energy bills, to be targeted at the most vulnerable. On the eve of the Budget, Healey said he wants to "start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good".The banks are braced for a levy or surcharge that may pay for this.There will be an announcement about further spending on defence, but not yet how spending 3% of national income on our security will be delivered by 2030 – that will come in next year's Spending Review.And one of the prime minister's key ideas - handing power away from Westminster and closer to you, devolution - will be central too.There will be, the chancellor told BBC Newscast, a "really radical devolution of powers and resources to local leaders that are often better placed to get beyond the departmental systems."But some at Westminster fret extra money for mayors and others in local government are not yet accompanied by adequate checks and balances to ensure that money is well spent.The chancellor will argue the economy is becoming more robust – and yes, there are some economic indicators that are more positive than forecast: growth is better than expected, as is productivity and unemployment is down.But as the Resolution Foundation think tank points out, external: "John Healey's problem is that conflict in the Middle East has once again pushed up energy prices and interest rates."So, despite the signs that the UK economy is becoming more resilient, household and public finances are in for another shock."In essence, we can expect a smaller Budget this time, compared to some in recent years, when it comes to the scale of tax and spending changes.The chancellor has been talking up a desire to offer "breathing space" and "hope" - a tacit acknowledgement that there is a limit to what the government can do given the constraints it faces.It has promised not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, a self imposed constraint, as the IFS put it. And there are the international ones beyond its control too.The big question for many will be whether the Budget is – or can be - big enough to meet the moment? Opposition parties will argue it amounts to tinkering.Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith argued the public finances are "on a cliff edge" and wants Healey to use the Budget to "take tough decisions, instead of continuing to kick the can down the road".For the Liberal Democrats, Daisy Cooper warned a "steady as she goes" Budget is "not going to cut it", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said the chancellor "can't keep fiddling while the economy burns". Green Party MP Ellie Chowns wanted a "bold" approach but fears it will be "business as usual".The government will try to convince you it is one of many moments in the coming weeks and months that will attempt to deliver the scale of change the prime minister has promised.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises

title: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJake HortonBBC VerifyPresident Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJake HortonBBC VerifyPresident Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, Trump has been casting doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting.However, studies suggest actual cases of these are extremely rare.BBC Verify has taken a look at the evidence and Trump's proposed changes to the voting system.How has Trump tried to change postal voting?For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.The majority of states allow, external people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.What is the SAVE America Act and what would it do?Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictionsHowever, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks, external.What does the evidence show on postal voting fraud?Studies of multiple US elections suggest postal vote fraud has been extremely rare.The Brookings Institute policy research think tank, external looked at the 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections and found an average of about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million postal votes.The report used a database kept by the Heritage Foundation - a think tank which has been aligned with Trump in the past - which records cases of electoral fraud that have ended in a conviction.We looked back in the database, external over the last 20 years and found it has tallied 325 convictions as a result of the fraudulent use of postal ballots.A 2020 study by the American Statistical Association, external looked at cases of voter fraud in eight states which send postal ballots to all eligible voters and found no evidence that voting by mail increased the risk of voter fraud overall.For example, according to the study, Oregon recorded 40 fraud cases between 2000 and 2020 having sent out more than 100 million postal ballots over that period.How has Trump tried to change voter ID rules?Trump has claimed non-citizen voting is widespread, and prior to the 2024 election he said Democrats were allowing millions of migrants into the US "so they can vote, vote, vote".It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in US federal elections - punishments can include a prison sentence, a fine, and deportation.The voting act the president has pushed Congress to pass would require voters to show a government-issued photo identification before they cast their ballots, as well as proof of citizenship when registering to vote and ongoing citizenship verification.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Millions of people have already voted early in the US midterm electionsCritics have raised concerns that stricter voter ID requirements could harm voter turnout as people may not have a passport or the required government-issued photo ID."We don't have a national ID card that the government gives out, unlike a lot of countries. Drivers licence is most common but it doesn't identify your immigration status so the ID that most Americans carry around wouldn't be enough for you to vote," says Jonathan Diaz, a voting rights expert at the Campaign Legal Center.Can illegal immigrants really vote in the US election?A 2023 survey by the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external suggested that about 21.3 million voting-age American citizens, or about 9%, do not have documents proving citizenship readily available.However, others argue that there has been no noticeable impact from existing voter ID laws."When scholars look at the effect of voter ID laws - either what the conservatives say on fraud or what progressive groups warn against about voter suppression - there doesn't seem to be a lot of proof that either has happened," says Walter Olson, an election expert at the conservative Cato Institute.A number of largely Republican-run states have tightened voter ID requirements in the last couple of years. There have been 21 restrictive voting laws enacted since the 2024 election to establish stricter ID requirements, according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice, external.What does the evidence show on non-citizens voting?Multiple studies show proven instances of non-citizens voting in past US elections have been very small.The Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.A 2026 analysis by Reuters, external of non-citizen voting cases brought in federal courts found that over the last 30 years 129 people have been criminally charged and 73 of those cases resulted in a conviction."The fact that it's illegal for non-citizens to vote is a pretty strong deterrent in the first place as many worry about their immigration status and it would be an extremely risky move to vote," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institute."There's never been any evidence that there are many people who have done that, certainly not enough to influence an election."What about non-citizens registered on voter rolls?Trump has also pushed for states to use a federal database - the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save) database - to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens and remove them from voter rolls.The tool has access to information about naturalised citizens and non-citizens who have contacted the federal government previously. It was launched in the 1980s to help government agencies verify individuals' eligibility for government benefits based on their immigration status.Critics have questioned the reliability of using the data to remove people from voter rolls as they say it could be outdated and include people who have since become US citizens - but the US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration using it this way.US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenshipImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Every US state allows some postal voting and 29% of voters cast a ballot that way in the 2024 presidential election"Federal databases can be invaluable to states trying to update their voter rolls so long as their limitations are understood," says Olson. "So part of the Trump plan which requires the sharing of information is positive, even if the second part to require states to treat the database contents as reliable despite their continuing evident gaps and inaccuracies is bad."The use of the programme by individual states is voluntary, and from those who have used it recently the number of non-citizens detected has been small.In Georgia, after an audit of the state's voter rolls, 432 possible non-citizens were identified, external on its voter rolls over 30 years.The Department of Homeland Security provided Nevada with a list of 185 names which it claimed identified non-citizens who had been improperly allowed to register to vote, but state officials found that they were all in fact citizens., externalThe White House has pointed to a case in New Jersey, where this summer a software glitch in the state's drivers licensing department registered about 6,600 non-citizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. State officials have said fewer than 400 cast ballots and they have all now been removed from the system.The US Justice Department requested that California doesn't count 20,000 postal ballots ahead of the midterms from people it claims are "likely non-citizen registrants" - but that request has been rejected by an appeals court.Out of that 20,000, it has charged 28 people, external who the department says are non-citizens who had illegally registered to vote.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare

title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
description: Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.Official data released in the
body: Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said."It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

schema.headline: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids

title: MS patient left in 'horrific' pain amid UK wide medicine shortage
description: Patient living in 'horrific pain' due to UK-wide drugs shortageImage caption, Jill Kenning experiences constant pain in her eye, which she compared to
body: Patient living in 'horrific pain' due to UK-wide drugs shortageImage caption, Jill Kenning experiences constant pain in her eye, which she compared to being "stabbed with a hot poker"ByToni Connor and Luke SprouleBBC News NIA woman with multiple sclerosis (MS) has said she is living with "horrific pain" after being unable to get a drug she uses to manage her condition.Jill Kenning has used Nabilone for 17 of the 18 years since she was diagnosed with MS and said the drug had been vital for managing her pain and helping her live a normal life.She said she had spent most of her time in bed since running out of the drug last Tuesday.Northern Ireland's devolved health department said there was disruption to supplies of the drug across the UK, meaning Nabilone was out of stock with wholesalers and not expected to be available again until December.A spokesperson said they would not say why there was disruption as the information was "commercially sensitive".According to a tracker published by the industry reference guide MIMS, the average number of drugs in short supply in the UK has trended upward this year, external.The number of drugs in short supply reached 157 this week, up from a low of 107 in January.Kenning, from Coleraine in County Londonderry, was diagnosed with MS in 2008 after experiencing problems with her sight.She subsequently developed numbness down the left side of her body and was treated by a neurologist.After a severe relapse, which resulted in a four-week hospital stay, she was prescribed Nabilone which she said made a massive difference to her quality of life."It helps me basically that I can get out of bed in the morning," she said.But she said that without the drug she experienced constant pain in her eye, which she compared to being "stabbed with a hot poker".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Earlier this year, pharmacists warned of medicine shortages in Northern IrelandAfter contacting her health trust for her regular repeat prescription, she said she was told there were no supplies of Nabilone available.She was told to contact her neurologist and has since been prescribed other medication.Kenning said the alternatives had not been effective and that her health had declined to the point where she had to stay in hospital for several nights."I don't want to be here any more because the pain is so bad," she said."I don't know how to describe it."I have been living on painkillers... I can't sleep, I'm sick, I'm not eating."Kenning said more should have been done to prepare patients for the disruption."How do I live my life? How do I cope with the pain?" she said."I'm not only fighting for me, I'm fighting for all the other patients that are on this drug."What is multiple sclerosis?Multiple sclerosis is a disease that affects nerves in the brain and spinal cord.The nerves in these areas are surrounded by a protein called myelin, which helps signals from the brain get to the rest of the body.The myelin becomes damaged in people with MS because the immune system mistakes it for something that shouldn't be there and attacks it.This means signals from the brain struggle to get through properly.What has the Department of Health said?Northern Ireland's Department of Health (DoH) said both licensed doses of Nabilone were out of stock from wholesalers across the UK.It said the shortage began affecting 1mg capsules in July, with the 0.25mg strength becoming unavailable more recently.The DoH said it was working with the UK's Department of Health and Social Care and health trusts to manage the disruption, and that guidance had been issued to healthcare professionals on alternative treatments, including unlicensed imports of Nabilone where available.A spokesperson said the DoH recognised "that medicine supply disruptions can be concerning for patients and the healthcare professionals who care for them"."If patients cannot access their prescribed medication or have concerns about an alternative, they should speak to their specialist healthcare teams for advice about their treatment options," the spokesperson said.Get in touchAre you affected by specific drug shortages? Share your experience.

schema.headline: MS patient left in 'horrific' pain amid UK wide medicine shortage

title: Drumcree: Judge to rule on Orangeman's challenge of march ban
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The parade in Portadown was banned after an intervention by Sir Chris BryantByCatherine DoyleBBC News NIUpdated 5
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The parade in Portadown was banned after an intervention by Sir Chris BryantByCatherine DoyleBBC News NIUpdated 5 minutes agoJudgment is due to be delivered later in a High Court bid to overturn the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant's decision to ban the Drumcree parade.The legal challenge was brought by a Portadown Orangeman against Sir Chris and the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher.Sir Chris's intervention to stop the parade came after he received security advice from Boutcher.The Drumcree dispute led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.The hearing is underway. Mr Justice Scoffield said he would rule on the matter on Wednesday morning.Before the parade was banned, the chief constable had written to Sir Chris stating: "The PSNI's current assessment is that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession have been exhausted."Any remaining options would require a substantial public order intervention and this is not assessed to be proportionate, and which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion affect across Northern Ireland."Last week, the court heard PSNI intelligence information that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on the police had officers cleared a path for the parade.The Garvaghy Road residents' case is that the Northern Ireland secretary's decision was lawful.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Orangemen made numerous attempts to begin their march but were blocked by police each timeWhat is the Drumcree dispute?The latest flare-up of the Drumcree dispute has featured a number of legal challenges, involving the Parades Commission, Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents. The dispute first came to prominence in the mid-1990s and almost derailed the Northern Ireland peace process at the time.When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order for the past three decades.The State of UsDrumcree explained: Provisional IRA and police notesLast month the Parades Commission decided that the march could go ahead on 27 September with restrictions in place after its original decision to stop the march was overturned in court.That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.An almost two-week-long stand-off began between protesters on the Garvaghy Road and members of the Orange Order and their supporters.Since Sir Chris's decision to ban the parade almost three weeks ago, the daily protests have dissipated with the action mostly moving to the courtroom.

schema.headline: Drumcree: Judge to rule on Orangeman's challenge of march ban

title: Jody Cundy bidding to go 20 years unbeaten at Para-cycling Track World Championships
description: Four laps, flat out, from a standing start. Legs and lungs screaming, lactic acid building.The kilo, track cycling's one-kilometre time trial, has a p
body: Four laps, flat out, from a standing start. Legs and lungs screaming, lactic acid building.The kilo, track cycling's one-kilometre time trial, has a punishing reputation.And yet Jody Cundy has been putting himself through it for decades."At the end of it, your legs don't want to pedal. You're fighting everything," he tells BBC Sport. "But when you get it right, it's really cool."Cundy is king of the kilo. At the Para-cycling Track World Championships, he has been unbeaten in the event since 2006.If he wins again at this year's edition - which starts on Thursday in Apeldoorn, the Netherlands - it will mark his 20th straight year in the rainbow jersey.Not bad for someone who has just turned 48 years old."It's a fairly dominant run," he said. "There have been some moments where I thought it wasn't going to happen and somehow I've pulled something out of the bag."But I am getting older and the competitors are getting younger. It's going to be very hard to keep that unbeaten run."As much as I would love to do it, the people I have to race this year...I'm in trouble."Some of that "trouble" comes from within the Great Britain squad.Archie Atkinson, 22, was eight years from being born when Cundy won his first Paralympic gold medal - as a swimmer - at Atlanta 1996. Atkinson was just two when Cundy first became world champion as a cyclist, after switching sports."One of my first races was against him," said Atkinson. "That felt pretty special."This guy was Paralympic champion, world champion and held a world record at the time."But Atkinson is catching up. Last year he beat Cundy at the National Track Championships, only to be beaten in turn by Cundy at the World Championships a few months later."I want to win," Atkinson said. "But if he wins, it's historic. There aren't many people who can win for 20 years."In addition to his world titles, Cundy is a six-time cycling Paralympic champion - two of those victories coming in the kilo, which he won at the 2008 and 2016 Games.Such is Cundy's standing in the squad that his team-mates call him "captain"."It feels like I've earned a bit of respect from being here for so long," he said. "I try to be the person everyone looks up to."But I know at some point somebody's going to have to take my place and I'll be walking away from the sport."When Cundy will walk away is anyone's guess.He says he doesn't have a plan for his retirement, but he knows that qualifying for the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles will be difficult."If I'm still performing at the very top level and that means that they want to take me, because I can go win in LA, then I shall be there and I'm there to be counted," he said."I'm realistic in the fact I'll be 49 when it comes to LA and I'm no spring chicken any more."What we do afterwards I really don't know, whether it's in sport in some way, shape or form."It's 31 years I've been in elite sport. If I go away and take all of that knowledge away with me, I feel like I'm kind of cheating the system a bit."So there's part of me that wants to come back and help - whether it's in a coaching role or a managerial role, or even further up in governing body roles and trying to influence the UCI [cycling's world governing body] and the IPC [International Paralympic Committee] - to make cycling better than what it actually is."The UCI, Cundy says, has "let the sport down" by the lack of Para-cycling track competitions it hosts outside of the World Championships and Paralympics.At the upcoming Worlds, Cundy and Atkinson are among a 24-strong Great Britain squad - but it is the first time the team will have raced at a UCI track event since the last edition of the Worlds in Brazil last year."When it comes to track cycling we have one race a year, the World Championships, and then every four years we have a [Paralympic] Games. That's really not good enough," he said."When I first started we used to have competitions, we used to travel and go race in places. Now you go 12 months without seeing anybody."You see a start list and you don't know who half of the names are on it. You don't know whether they're going to be fast, slow, whether they're any good. There's not really any results or rankings to follow."The UCI did not respond to a request for comment.

schema.headline: Jody Cundy bidding to go 20 years unbeaten at Para-cycling Track World Championships

title: Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority
description: With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predic
body: With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predicted with his Likud emerging as the largest single party.His existing bloc with ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties appear to be just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. However, analysts caution that this is subject to change because the early count was skewed towards areas known to have strong right-wing support.A dramatic deadlock had been widely forecast as Israelis surged to the polls – with turnout reaching more than 77%.In Israel's fragmented political system, the signs are that Netanyahu's main rival, the former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, would struggle to command a parliamentary majority without parties led by Israel's Arab minority. According to partial results, they have equalled or gained on their previous record number of seats.On the campaign trail, most Jewish opposition parties pledged not to work with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values.However, Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if others were prepared to join forces with them. In this election, Arab Israelis – who often identify  as Palestinian citizens of Israel and represent one-fifth of the population – appeared to turn out in unprecedented numbers. Many saw this as a make-or-break election to defeat Israel's most right-wing-ever government, accusing it of stoking racism and hatred.A huge caveat in all of the current analysis is that the high number of as-yet-uncounted absentee ballots – mostly representing the votes of Israeli soldiers – mean that we are not expecting to have a clear idea of the final results for another day or two.Overnight, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot addressed their supporters, pledging to form the next government."The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and all those who support the Jewish state. That is what has become clear. A decisive majority," the PM told his celebrating supporters – although he stopped short of declaring victory."We must form a strong, national, right-wing government. That is what must be done," he added."The public has chosen change," Eisenkot told his Yashar party after exit polls came out – most of which were initially more favourable to the opposition. "The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust. The Israeli public voted against Benjamin Netanyahu continuing as prime minister.""I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israeli's citizens.  And quickly – because that is what this moment demands, and because the country needs to be brought back together."There are deep divisions in Israeli society which have been underscored by this and previous elections. They have served not just as referenda on Netanyahu's leadership – as he faces a corruption trial on charges he denies – but also as votes on what kind of country Israel should be.The PM and his current coalition partners have taken the country on a hardline religious, nationalist trajectory over the past four years. There were mass protests over their plan for a judicial overhaul prior to the unprecedented Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023 which triggered a series of wars – in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.Many Israelis want to see their country more firmly anchored in liberal and secular values.Remarkably, the past four turbulent years do not appear to have significantly changed voting patterns. "We see in the polls, that the relative weight of the two main sides: pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu is about the same," Professor Tamar Hermann, a pollster at the Israeli Democracy Institute told me, just prior to the election.  "People expected that after October 7th, Netanyahu will be down the drain or even toppled but it didn't happen."Already, overnight, the main Israeli parties will have begun their intense political wrangling to try to form a new coalition government."Each side will try to pull over defectors, or will try to see if they can make a minority government and will try all these different political kinds of wizardry," is how veteran Israeli journalist and author, Yaakov Katz described the process to me.  "But it might not work, and it could take weeks or months to see if someone is actually capable of forming a government."The leaders of the bigger parties typically try to win over smaller ones with promises of cabinet positions, budgets or specific policies.It is key now to see if those in the main opposition "change bloc" are ready to break a taboo by seeking a political deal with the Arab parties.On the campaign trail, one of the bloc's leaders, right-wing politician Avigdor Lieberman, went as far as to say that he would not sit in a minority government that relied on their support.  It was a sign of the increased mistrust and hostility towards Arab citizens since the 7 October assault.When I recently met Mansour Abbas, head of Ra'am – the smaller of the two Arab lists – he told me that having been part of the diverse coalition that temporarily unseated Netanyahu between 2021 and 2022, he wanted to join the next government. He believed that potential partners would be more open to an alliance after the election."These are familiar and well-known party-political considerations. All politicians in Israel say one thing before elections and speak a different language after elections," he said. "We have experienced this before, and it does not concern us."Meanwhile, Netanyahu and his allies have already begun an intense campaign of delegitimising the Arab parties – casting their fellow citizens as a threat from within.So what are the next steps?After the final results are presented to Israel's largely ceremonial president, Isaac Herzog, next week, he will consult all the leaders of elected parties and ask the candidate who appears most likely to form a coalition to do so.If that candidate is unable to pull together a majority within a maximum of six weeks, then others could be allowed to try.If, after all the haggling, no-one is able to form a governing coalition, a new election will be held in the following months, and the entire process will be repeated.In the meantime, Netanyahu's government stays on in a caretaker role but without the authority to enact major policy changes.

schema.headline: Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority

title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
description: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentWe're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.That is the cash buffer the gove
body: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentWe're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.1. Increase taxes on banksBanks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money.And there is widespread belief among bank bosses that the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget.Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates, external that increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additional £1bn to £2bn a year for the Treasury.2. Higher taxes on gambling machinesFormer Prime Minister Gordon Brown has called on Healey to hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.The Social Market Foundation (SMF) think tank has estimated, external that doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between £275m and £460m - depending on how gamblers reacted to it.People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.3. Get online marketplaces to collect VATReports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms.The Treasury estimates it is missing out on around £12bn a year, external in VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year.Amazon, which supports the move, has estimated it could raise £700m, external a year in VAT for the government.Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.4. Cut welfare spendingThe above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around £3.5bn a year.That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits.The Conservatives claim they could make savings of £36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments.Reform say they would save £50bn a year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings.Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from £68bn this year to £81bn in 2031.Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves attempted to reduce spending on these benefits , externalby £5bn a year by 2030, but were forced to reverse course after a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.Cuts to health and disability welfare would reduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments, external and/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.Graphics by Callum Thomson and Lewis McBlane.Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax

title: Losing both legs ended my football dream - now skiing gives me freedom
description: Image source, Adam GolebiewskiImage caption, Adam Golebiewski has been able to train in snowByLouise HosieBBC ScotlandReporting fromHuntly and Ken Ban
body: Image source, Adam GolebiewskiImage caption, Adam Golebiewski has been able to train in snowByLouise HosieBBC ScotlandReporting fromHuntly and Ken BanksNorth east Scotland reporterUpdated 3 hours agoA promising footballer who lost both legs after a car crash has a new passion in life - after finding "freedom" in skiing.Adam Golebiewski was only 17 when the crash happened in 2024 in Macduff, Aberdeenshire. He needed a double amputation below the knee.The former goalkeeper celebrated his 18th birthday during his rehabilitation in hospital, and was fitted for prosthetics. Since then he has become a father, and - now aged 20 - is showing a flair for para cross-country skiing. Adam's coach thinks the Parlaympic Winter Games could be a target.Adam faced three months of rehabilitation at Woodend Hospital in Aberdeen following the crash which was caused by a drink driver. He was able to walk again on crutches, and was "thankful and grateful" to be home with his family that Christmas.Adam's dreams of becoming a professional goalkeeper were shattered, but in the face of adversity he found a new joy.He now trains at the Nordic ski centre in Huntly, next to the field where he used to play football with junior side Deveronside. There, he uses a special sit-ski with a board and wheels. The board is replaced with skis when he trains on snow - something he had the chance to do in America earlier this year.With no previous experience of the sport, he has just qualified to enter international competitions as a para biathlete - which combines cross-country skiing and shooting.Figure caption, 'I don't think of my injuries when I am on the board'His sights are now set on para biathlon World Cup events in Finland and Sweden over the next six months."I don't actually think of my injuries when I'm on the board - I just forget that I have them," he told BBC Scotland News."I just feel so free and I just forget about everything else."Of his training travels, he explained: "In Colorado, I didn't really know anybody and I was quite nervous to go and try it out, but once I was on the snow I was completely fine - even though I fell about 40 times."Then Italy, that was another good experience where I I tried biathlon, which is skiing and shooting."The last trip I was recently on was Oberhof in Germany which was again just an improvement from the first time being away on snow, and I learned a lot more again."He said his mind was "completely focused" on what he is doing.Image caption, Adam needed a double amputation as a teenager two years agoAdam's coach, Simon Bate of Snowsport Scotland, said he had made impressive progress.Bate believes the Parlaympic Winter Games in 2030 could be a future goal."From when I first met him as an 18-year-old and he just had this real maturity and positive outlook," he said."He's always been very very up for what we've suggested in terms of the training, he's really keen to work hard."Image caption, Adam has mainly been training on wheelsBate added: "He's definitely got the potential - and I think he's going to do well."Adam hopes to be an inspiration to others facing difficult times."I think they should just give it a go because you never know what could happen," he said."Since I've started skiing, I've loved every minute of it."I never knew any of this would happen so quickly. It's just given me a bit of freedom again."Image source, Adam GolebiewskiImage caption, Adam says he hopes to be an inspiration to othersA drink-driver who caused the crash in which Adam was injured was later detained for 32 months.Arran Paterson, 19, admitted causing serious injury by dangerous driving, being over the drink-drive limit, and driving without insurance.Adam had been a passenger in Paterson's car which crashed into a wall. Two other teenage passengers were also seriously injured.Patterson was also disqualified from driving for five years and four months.

schema.headline: Losing both legs ended my football dream - now skiing gives me freedom

title: Stan Wawrinka retires: Three-time Grand Slam champion's career ends with Basel defeat
description: Whether through technique or toil, Stan Wawrinka has always been able to whip fans into a frenzy.The ability to stir the emotions of a crowd never lef
body: Whether through technique or toil, Stan Wawrinka has always been able to whip fans into a frenzy.The ability to stir the emotions of a crowd never left him - even in what proved to be the final tour-level match of the 41-year-old Swiss star's glorious career.Former world number three Wawrinka might have lost to Czech opponent Jiri Lehecka in front of passionate home support in Basel on Tuesday, but he did not wave farewell without showing the hallmarks of a stunning career that exceeded expectations.The stylish one-handed backhand down the line. The finger pointing to the temple. The demand for more noise from the stands.The roar of "Allez!" after winning a point he probably should not have won.The temptation to snap his racquet over his knee after missing a shot he felt he should have made.There were tears, too, of course.Wawrinka, his family, and his team were dabbing their eyes once the reality of an honourable 7-5 7-6 (7-2) defeat dawned.It meant a professional career spanning 23 years, 985 matches and three Grand Slam titles was over."All I wanted in my career was to give everything, have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100% in every match - out of respect for myself, the opponent, the tournament, the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP website., external"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and the only way you can leave the sport - without any regrets."Wawrinka is loved by millions of fans because he is relatable - an everyman personality who reached the pinnacle of his sport by pushing himself to the limit.So many talented players of his generation lamented the presence of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, believing the 'Big Three' to be a blockade preventing them from becoming a Grand Slam champion.It did not stop Wawrinka. With explosive shot-making, relentless endurance and indomitable spirit, he barrelled past the trio of superstars on his way to winning his trio of majors.Wawrinka had been a player whose career was ticking along steadily, rather than spectacularly, until he lifted one of the sport's biggest prizes at the age of 28.Seeded eighth at the 2014 Australian Open, he saw off Djokovic in the quarter-finals before completing an unforeseen triumph against top seed Nadal."I never expected to win a Grand Slam because, for me, I was not good enough to beat those guys," Wawrinka admitted as he clutched the trophy in Melbourne.In fact, he was more than good enough - proving it again and again.At the 2015 French Open, Wawrinka brushed past Swiss compatriot Federer in the quarter-finals, then demolished Djokovic in the final with a display of unrelenting power - a performance which must be ranked among the greatest of his era. His last major title arrived at the 2016 US Open, when he escaped from match point down against Britain's Dan Evans in the third round and went on to beat Djokovic for the title.It is little wonder that 24-time major champion Djokovic - considered by many the greatest player of all-time - described Wawrinka as a "legend"."Stan's had an incredible career. The competitor he is on court, talent, strength, power, precision - he had it all," said the 39-year-old Serb, who practised with Wawrinka in Basel.Wawrinka was good enough to win majors, but he wasn't as consistently good as his illustrious rivals.The 'Big Three' is often expanded to a 'Big Four' featuring Britain's three-time major champion Andy Murray, who soared to world number one, won two Olympic singles gold medals and lifted the ATP Finals trophy.Wawrinka recognises he was "really far" from creating a 'Big Five' - and the evidence underlines that.Spending 267 weeks in the top 10, winning one Masters 1,000 tournament and claiming 15 other tour-level titles is well below Federer, Nadal, Djokovic and Murray, but it is also more than most players can dream of achieving.The Grand Slam triumphs are what really set Wawrinka apart from most peers - and, coupled with his commendable attitude, is why 'Stan the Man' will be remembered for emerging as a great himself in a golden generation where others came up short.

schema.headline: Stan Wawrinka retires: Three-time Grand Slam champion's career ends with Basel defeat

title: Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal (5-3 on pens): Where does it rank among best cup upsets?
description: Where does Fleetwood beating Arsenal rank in biggest cup upsets?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fleetwood Town reached the League Cup quarter
body: Where does Fleetwood beating Arsenal rank in biggest cup upsets?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fleetwood Town reached the League Cup quarter-finals for the first time by beating ArsenalArsenal suffered a shock Carabao Cup exit at the home of Fleetwood Town, as the League Two side recorded one of the biggest upsets in the competition's history.Mikel Arteta's Premier League champions lost 5-3 on penalties to a Fleetwood outfit ranked 84 places below them in the English football pyramid.Following Fleetwood's victory, BBC Sport looks at some of the biggest shocks of all-time in the FA Cup and League Cup.This isn't an exhaustive list, and you can leave your thoughts in the comments, rank the historic upsets and share your results.Fleetwood Town celebrated the biggest victory in the club's history as they stunned Champions League finalists Arsenal to reach the EFL Cup quarter-finals at Highbury Stadium.The League Two club stunned the visitors when Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave Fleetwood, who sat 19th in English football's fourth tier, a 21st-minute lead.Viktor Gyokeres pulled Arsenal level after the break - but they could not kick on and were reduced to 10 men in the 86th minute when teenager Max Dowman kicked out following a challenge by Harrison Neal.In the shootout, Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch saved Bruno Guimaraes' spot kick before Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty to spark scenes of ecstasy on the pitch and in the stands.Grimsby 2-2 Man Utd (12-11 on pens, League Cup, 2025)An upset as astonishing for its manner as it was for its proportions. Grimsby Town, a League Two side, beat top-flight Manchester United.Not only did they win against Ruben Amorim's side, but they were 2-0 up after 30 minutes following goals from Charles Vernam and Tyrell Warren.The visitors pulled one back through Bryan Mbeumo with 15 minutes to go and United looked like they might squeeze through when Harry Maguire went on to level in the 89th minute.But an incredible shootout followed, with Clarke Oduor for Grimsby and Matheus Cunha for Manchester United missing the only penalties as each side's 11 took one.The players then went again and, after Darragh Burns scored to make it 12-11, Mbeumo struck his second spot-kick against the crossbar.Plymouth 1-0 Liverpool (FA Cup, 2025)Arne Slot made 10 changes to his Liverpool side after they had won an EFL Cup semi-final in their previous game and the Reds were made to pay.Eight minutes after the interval, the Pilgrims were awarded a penalty after Harvey Elliott's handball and Ryan Hardie drilled home from the spot in emphatic fashion.Hardie almost added a second shortly afterwards when his shot was turned on to the post by Liverpool keeper Caoimhin Kelleher.The bottom club in the Championship held on, with Conor Hazard making crucial late saves, to beat a team who would go on to win the Premier League title.Chelsea 2-4 Bradford City (FA Cup, 2015)Bradford ranked 49 places below their opponents as they travelled to Stamford Bridge to take on Chelsea, who at that point were top of the Premier League.Gary Cahill and Ramires netted to put the hosts 2-0 up and give Chelsea firm control of the fourth-round tie.Bradford had other ideas, though, as Jon Stead pulled one back before Filipe Morais side-footed in an equaliser.Andy Halliday then blasted the Bantams ahead before Mark Yeats slotted a fourth to inflict a crushing defeat on Jose Mourinho's side.Oldham 3-2 Liverpool (FA Cup, 2013)Premier League giants Liverpool had ample strength at Boundary Park, with the likes of Luis Suarez, Raheem Sterling and Daniel Sturridge all starting.League One hosts Oldham were in the midst of financial problems but produced a spirited display against the odds, with Matt Smith nodding in a Youssouf M'Changama cross to open the scoring.Suarez levelled, but Smith soon took advantage of an error from Liverpool goalkeeper Brad Jones before Reece Wabara netted a back-post header to give the Latics a 3-1 lead.Joe Allen volleyed home to pull one back and Liverpool brought on Steven Gerrard, but it was not enough to avoid defeat.Bradford City 1-1 Arsenal (3-2 on pens, League Cup, 2012)A fourth-tier side against Premier League opposition in the quarter-finals of the league cup - Arsenal were clear favourites.Bradford had already caused an upset in the tournament, beating Wigan on penalties in the round before. Up for a fight at home to Arsene Wenger's Gunners, Garry Thompson volleyed the Bantams ahead before Thomas Vermaelen headed home a Santi Cazorla cross with just two minutes of normal time remaining.Just as Mbeumo missed the decisive kick for United against Grimsby after scoring in normal time, the same happened for Vermaelen here as Bradford prevailed 3-2 on spot-kicks.Liverpool 2-2 Northampton (2-4 on pens, League Cup, 2010)Another surprise cup exit for Liverpool.This one happened in the League Cup - at Anfield. Milan Jovanovic fired in an opener for Liverpool, but Billy McKay equalised and Michael Jacobs tapped in to give the Cobblers a lead early in extra time.David Ngog scored from a late header to set up the penalty drama, but Northampton were the victors from the spot, with Abdul Osman keeping his cool to slot in the decisive spot-kick.Man Utd 0-3 York City (League Cup, 1995)Ruben Amorim at Grimsby was not the first Manchester United to suffer a shock in the League Cup - even Sir Alex Ferguson has faced the same.The United boss didn't take the game lightly and made just four changes from the league game which they had played three days before, with the likes of David Beckham, Lee Sharpe and Ryan Giggs starting.Paul Barnes, father of Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes, scored twice for Alan Little's visitors, including one from the penalty spot, before Tony Barras headed a third to inflict a crushing defeat at Old Trafford.United put out another strong team at Bootham Crescent for the return leg two weeks later, with Eric Cantona in their squad, but despite getting two goals from Paul Scholes and another from Terry Cooke, the Minstermen went through 4-3 on aggregate thanks to a strike from Scott Jordan.Wrexham 2-1 Arsenal (FA Cup, 1992)Arsenal were reigning First Division champions and second in the top flight.Wrexham had finished 24th in the Fourth Division in the previous season.The Gunners made the trip to Wales as firm favourites and were just 10 minutes from securing a spot in the fourth round after Alan Smith's first-half opener.But Mickey Thomas sent a 25-yard free kick past David Seaman before Steve Watkin's strike earned victory for Wrexham just two minutes later.Sutton 2-1 Coventry (FA Cup, 1989)Sutton United had a memorable cup run in 2016-17, beating three EFL teams - including Leeds United - before losing to Arsenal in the fifth round.They have also produced one of the biggest shocks of all time.The non-league side took on a Coventry team who were then in the First Division and had won the FA Cup in 1987.The part-time side upset the odds at home, with Matthew Hanlan volleying home the winner just before the hour mark.Hereford 2-1 Newcastle (FA Cup, 1972)Top-flight Newcastle were beaten in the third round of the FA Cup by non-league opposition when they took on Hereford United in 1972.Hereford took the tie to a replay after a 2-2 draw at St James' Park, but Newcastle looked destined to make it to the fourth round thanks to a late goal by Malcolm McDonald in the rematch.However, the non-leaguers had other ideas and Ronnie Radford popped up to score the most famous 30-yard goal in FA Cup history to take the game into extra time.Substitute Ricky George scored the winner - amid scenes of wild celebration at Edgar Street - as Hereford became the first non-league club to defeat a First Division side since 1949.

schema.headline: Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal (5-3 on pens): Where does it rank among best cup upsets?

title: Fleetwood Town: League Two club fearless for EFL Cup quarter-final after Arsenal upset
description: Given their league positions, form and pedigree, there could surely only have been one winner.Fleetwood played Arsenal on Tuesday with an 84-place gul
body: Given their league positions, form and pedigree, there could surely only have been one winner.Fleetwood played Arsenal on Tuesday with an 84-place gulf between the teams and most home fans arriving in hope rather than expectation. But remarkably, it was the hosts who booked their place in the Carabao Cup quarter-final thanks to their penalty shootout win over the Gunners.For the side known as the Cod Army, who won six promotions in 12 years in an impressive journey from non-league, this result will surely be remembered longest of all. Against the reigning Premier League champions, the club from a small seaside town in Lancashire created history in claiming one of the biggest cup upsets ever.Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave the hosts the lead after 21 minutes but, after the break, Viktor Gyokeres pulled the visitors level.And from there, they might have been expected to take charge, but Fleetwood remained resolute, prospering from a wasteful performance from Arsenal that included Max Dowman being sent off for kicking out after a robust challenge from Harrison Neal.Fleetwood, who sit 18th in League Two having won just once in their past eight league games, dared to dream and took the game to penalties, with fans spilling on to the pitch after Conor Haughey's decisive spot-kick."The biggest night in the club's history in terms of opposition coming to town and we've managed to beat the champions," boss Matt Lawlor told Sky Sports in the aftermath of his side's stunning victory."I'm a big football fan and I watch National League all the way through to the Premier League, Championship. So for me it was a tough game to prepare for, but I'm just so glad that the lads have the feeling the way they are and took that performance in to make that town, the club, everyone proud."Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, left-back Jake Batty added: "Our league form's not been as good as what we'd want it to be and for some reason [in] cup competitions everyone gets a bit of a fire in their belly. We just came up with some magical moments and obviously that's one to tell the grandkids, isn't it?"We've struggled. We're not known as a big club in League Two. We get a few thousand fans each game, and just the buzz around the town, you could see the fans in the shootout and all game."That's what we encourage to bring on Saturday. That's what we want on Saturday."Why can't we replicate that and get 5,000 fans behind us every game and, and give us that momentum?"Batty added that on reaching the quarter-finals for the first time since their arrival in the English Football League in 2012, Fleetwood should be "fearless" and hope for a home tie."It's unbelievable for the town and hopefully we can get someone else at home and do exactly the same thing," he said."I don't think we should be scared of any team."On 20 April 2024, Fleetwood's relegation from League One was confirmed, capping off a miserable season for the club on the pitch.That same day, Arsenal beat Wolves 2-0 at Molineux to go top of the Premier League. They would finish that campaign second, but won the title two years later.Meanwhile, Fleetwood have held their heads above water in League Two - and the league is very much in mind for boss Lawlor, with his side facing Bristol Rovers on Saturday."It's really hard to address the players. I've just said to enjoy it and then we've got a league game on Saturday," he added."I didn't want to be the bearer of the reality, but we've got a game."It was Haughey who ultimately struck the winning penalty to send the hosts through, yet it was goalkeeper Jay Lynch who tipped the shootout in their favour.He pulled off superb saves during the match to deny Ben White and Martin Odegaard, then kept out Bruno Guimaraes' penalty, and was left hoarse in the aftermath of a stunning victory at a windy Highbury.It was a victory which he likened to Grimsby's triumph over Manchester United in the competition last season."My voice has gone from organising the defence," Lynch told Sky Sports."We took heart from Grimsby beating Man United last year. We kind of compared it."It was a typical night in Fleetwood. We were expecting a storm, we knew the conditions would be horrible, so we thought it might go in our favour."It's amazing for the club, the town. Honestly it means everything to everyone."

schema.headline: Fleetwood Town: League Two club fearless for EFL Cup quarter-final after Arsenal upset

title: What do you want from the Budget? 'I get £4,062 a year and am trying my best'
description: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma Crew
body: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma CrewUpdated 28 October 2026 00:03 GMTChancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice.Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college. The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers."I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee, external scheme extended.The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."'I earn £30,000 and dread filling up my car'Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump."The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, and the BBC understands it will be frozen again, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."'I earn £22,000. Saving for a house is impossible'Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.   "Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax. He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently. He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."'I earn £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40'Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living. She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity."We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, the £250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as £50.Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families."I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."'I earn £150,000 and would be happy to pay more tax'Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year."I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors."If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."'I have a £15,000 pension. I'm spending more of my savings'Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her. "It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look at removing standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit, external, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: What do you want from the Budget? 'I get £4,062 a year and am trying my best'

title: Carabao Cup: Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal (5-3 pens): Max Dowman sees red as Arsenal dumped out, did Arteta go too far?
description: Max Dowman has been getting used to making headlines for moments of magic, but the 16-year-old was in the spotlight for the wrong reasons when he was
body: Max Dowman has been getting used to making headlines for moments of magic, but the 16-year-old was in the spotlight for the wrong reasons when he was sent off as Arsenal suffered a shock loss to Fleetwood Town.Dowman scored twice as Arsenal beat Ipswich in the previous round of the Carabao Cup and manager Mikel Arteta rewarded him with another start in the Gunners' last-16 tie.And this one was perhaps more of an opportunity than it looked.
